claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Furtado et al., 2011.

claims.claim: T. gondii is a leading cause of infectious retinochoroiditis.
claims.source: Additionally, T. gondii is a leading cause of infectious retinochoroiditis (Weiss and Dubey, 2009).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Weiss and Dubey, 2009.

claims.claim: Eye disease from T. gondii is most prominent in Latin America and Africa.
claims.source: Eye disease is most prominent in Latin America and Africa with approximately one-third of uveitis cases being attributed to ocular toxoplasmosis (Furtado et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Furtado et al., 2013.

claims.claim: Approximately one-third of uveitis cases are attributed to ocular toxoplasmosis.
claims.source: Eye disease is most prominent in Latin America and Africa with approximately one-third of uveitis cases being attributed to ocular toxoplasmosis (Furtado et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Furtado et al., 2013.

claims.claim: Mechanisms of immune control of T. gondii are well studied in the mouse.
claims.source: Although mechanisms of immune control are well studied in the mouse, they are less well understood in humans with currently known mechanisms of restriction observed in a cell type-dependent manner (Fisch et al., 2019b).
claims.evidence: This is a general statement about the state of knowledge in the field, supported by citation.

claims.claim: Mechanisms of immune control of T. gondii are less well understood in humans than in mice.
claims.source: Although mechanisms of immune control are well studied in the mouse, they are less well understood in humans with currently known mechanisms of restriction observed in a cell type-dependent manner (Fisch et al., 2019b).
claims.evidence: This is a general statement about the state of knowledge in the field, supported by citation.

claims.claim: Currently known mechanisms of T. gondii restriction in humans are observed in a cell type-dependent manner.
claims.source: Although mechanisms of immune control are well studied in the mouse, they are less well understood in humans with currently known mechanisms of restriction observed in a cell type-dependent manner (Fisch et al., 2019b).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Fisch et al., 2019b.

claims.claim: Host cells express and secrete interferons in response to pathogen infection.
claims.source: In response to pathogen infection, host cells express and secrete interferons (IFNs), which signal in an autocrine or paracrine manner through IFN receptors to induce factors designed to block infection.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about the innate immune response.

claims.claim: Interferons signal in an autocrine or paracrine manner through IFN receptors.
claims.source: In response to pathogen infection, host cells express and secrete interferons (IFNs), which signal in an autocrine or paracrine manner through IFN receptors to induce factors designed to block infection.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about interferon signaling.

claims.claim: Interferons fall into three categories: type I (including IFNα and IFNβ), type II (IFNγ), and type III (IFNλ1–4).
claims.source: Interferons fall into three categories: type I (including IFNα and IFNβ), type II (IFNγ), and type III (IFNλ1–4).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about interferon classification.

claims.claim: Receptors for type I and type II IFN are ubiquitously expressed.
claims.source: In general, receptors for type I and type II IFN are ubiquitously expressed whereas type III IFN sensitivity is restricted to epithelial barriers.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about interferon receptor expression.

claims.claim: Type III IFN sensitivity is restricted to epithelial barriers.
claims.source: In general, receptors for type I and type II IFN are ubiquitously expressed whereas type III IFN sensitivity is restricted to epithelial barriers.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about type III interferon receptor expression.

claims.claim: IFN signaling conventionally involves the induction of interferon-stimulated genes (ISGs) involved in host defense via JAK-STAT-mediated signaling.
claims.source: Conventionally, IFN signaling involves the induction of interferon-stimulated genes (ISGs) involved in host defense via JAK-STAT-mediated signaling (Alspach et al., 2019; Lazear et al., 2019; Schoggins, 2019).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Alspach et al., 2019; Lazear et al., 2019; Schoggins, 2019.

claims.claim: Induction of ISGs is only semi-conserved between cell types, with many ISGs being cell type dependent.
claims.source: Although IFN upregulates the expression of many genes, induction of ISGs is only semi-conserved between cell types, with many ISGs being cell type dependent (Schoggins, 2019).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Schoggins, 2019.

claims.claim: Variability in ISG expression may be due to the induction of noncanonical IFN signaling pathways that have been observed in a cell type-dependent manner.
claims.source: Variability in ISG expression is perhaps due to the induction of noncanonical IFN signaling pathways that have been observed in a cell type-dependent manner (Van Boxel-Dezaire and Stark, 2007; van Boxel-Dezaire et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Van Boxel-Dezaire and Stark, 2007; van Boxel-Dezaire et al., 2006.

claims.claim: Interferon gamma (IFNγ) has been known since the 1980s to be expressed during T. gondii infection.
claims.source: Interferon gamma (IFNγ) has been known since the 1980s to be expressed during T. gondii infection and to be critical for restricting infection in mice (Suzuki et al., 1988; McCabe et al., 1984; Shirahata and Shimizu, 1980).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Suzuki et al., 1988; McCabe et al., 1984; Shirahata and Shimizu, 1980.

claims.claim: IFNγ is critical for restricting T. gondii infection in mice.
claims.source: Interferon gamma (IFNγ) has been known since the 1980s to be expressed during T. gondii infection and to be critical for restricting infection in mice (Suzuki et al., 1988; McCabe et al., 1984; Shirahata and Shimizu, 1980).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Suzuki et al., 1988; McCabe et al., 1984; Shirahata and Shimizu, 1980.

claims.claim: IFNγ-mediated restriction in mice has been attributed to the expression of immunity-related GTPases (IRGs) and guanylate binding proteins (GBPs).
claims.source: IFNγ-mediated restriction has been attributed to the expression of a group of ISGs, including immunity-related GTPases (IRGs) and guanylate binding proteins (GBPs) (Gazzinelli et al., 2014; MacMicking, 2012).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Gazzinelli et al., 2014; MacMicking, 2012.

claims.claim: IRGs and GBPs are recruited to the parasitophorous vacuole membrane (PVM) resulting in a loss of membrane integrity and parasite death.
claims.source: IRGs and GBPs are recruited to the parasitophorous vacuole membrane (PVM) resulting in a loss of membrane integrity and parasite death (Ling et al., 2006; Martens et al., 2005; Yamamoto et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Ling et al., 2006; Martens et al., 2005; Yamamoto et al., 2012.

claims.claim: Type I and type II strains of T. gondii express the Ser/Thr kinase ROP18.
claims.source: As a defense, type I and type II strains of T. gondii express the Ser/Thr kinase ROP18, which phosphorylates and inactivates IRG proteins to prevent PVM damage (Hunter and Sibley, 2012; Mukhopadhyay et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Hunter and Sibley, 2012; Mukhopadhyay et al., 2020.

claims.claim: ROP18 phosphorylates and inactivates IRG proteins to prevent PVM damage.
claims.source: As a defense, type I and type II strains of T. gondii express the Ser/Thr kinase ROP18, which phosphorylates and inactivates IRG proteins to prevent PVM damage (Hunter and Sibley, 2012; Mukhopadhyay et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Hunter and Sibley, 2012; Mukhopadhyay et al., 2020.

claims.claim: Increased nitric oxide production due to induction of inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS) plays a role in restricting T. gondii infection in mice in vivo and in vitro.
claims.source: Additionally, increased nitric oxide production due to induction of inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS) has also been shown to play a role in restricting T. gondii infection in mice in vivo and in vitro (Khan et al., 1997; Adams et al., 1990; Meisel et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Khan et al., 1997; Adams et al., 1990; Meisel et al., 2011.

claims.claim: IFNγ is important for T. gondii restriction in human cells in vitro.
claims.source: IFNγ is similarly important for T. gondii restriction in human cells in vitro and IFNγ expression has been shown to correlate with disease severity in vivo (Pfefferkorn et al., 1986; Meira et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Pfefferkorn et al., 1986; Meira et al., 2014.

claims.claim: IFNγ expression has been shown to correlate with disease severity in vivo in humans.
claims.source: IFNγ is similarly important for T. gondii restriction in human cells in vitro and IFNγ expression has been shown to correlate with disease severity in vivo (Pfefferkorn et al., 1986; Meira et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Pfefferkorn et al., 1986; Meira et al., 2014.

claims.claim: Humans possess one truncated IRG that likely lacks GTPase activity.
claims.source: Humans possess one truncated IRG that likely lacks GTPase activity and only one nontruncated IRG that is not IFNγ or infection inducible (Bekpen et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Bekpen et al., 2005.

claims.claim: Humans possess only one nontruncated IRG that is not IFNγ or infection inducible.
claims.source: Humans possess one truncated IRG that likely lacks GTPase activity and only one nontruncated IRG that is not IFNγ or infection inducible (Bekpen et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Bekpen et al., 2005.

claims.claim: It is unlikely IRGs play a role in human resistance to T. gondii infection.
claims.source: Hence, it is unlikely IRGs play a role in human resistance to T. gondii infection.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the limited IRG repertoire in humans.

claims.claim: Human GBP1 restricts T. gondii infection in a cell type-dependent manner.
claims.source: Although human GBP1 has been shown to restrict T. gondii infection, it does so in a cell type-dependent manner. GBP1 restricts infection in IFNγ-treated human mesenchymal stromal cells (MSCs) and lung epithelial cells (i.e., A549 cells) but not myeloid-derived cells (i.e., HAP1 cells) (Qin et al., 2017; Ohshima et al., 2014; Johnston et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Qin et al., 2017; Ohshima et al., 2014; Johnston et al., 2016.

claims.claim: GBP1 restricts T. gondii infection in IFNγ-treated human mesenchymal stromal cells (MSCs) and lung epithelial cells (A549 cells) but not myeloid-derived cells (HAP1 cells).
claims.source: GBP1 restricts infection in IFNγ-treated human mesenchymal stromal cells (MSCs) and lung epithelial cells (i.e., A549 cells) but not myeloid-derived cells (i.e., HAP1 cells) (Qin et al., 2017; Ohshima et al., 2014; Johnston et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Qin et al., 2017; Ohshima et al., 2014; Johnston et al., 2016.

claims.claim: GBP1 is implicated in an inflammasome pathway that results in host cell death in human macrophages following T. gondii infection.
claims.source: GBP1 is also implicated in an inflammasome pathway that results in host cell death in human macrophages following T. gondii infection (Fisch et al., 2019a).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Fisch et al., 2019a.

claims.claim: GBP5 plays a role in the clearance of T. gondii from human macrophages in vitro in an IFNγ independent manner.
claims.source: Additionally, GBP5 has been shown to play a role in the clearance of T. gondii from human macrophages in vitro, albeit in an IFNγ independent manner (Matta et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Matta et al., 2018.

claims.claim: Humans possess an ISG15-dependent, IFNγ inducible, noncanonical autophagy (ATG) pathway that restricts T. gondii growth in human cervical adenocarcinoma cells (HeLa cells) and A549 cells.
claims.source: Humans also possess an ISG15-dependent, IFNγ inducible, noncanonical autophagy (ATG) pathway that restricts T. gondii growth in human cervical adenocarcinoma cells (HeLa cells) and A549 cells (Bhushan et al., 2020; Selleck et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Bhushan et al., 2020; Selleck et al., 2015.

claims.claim: A similar noncanonical ATG dependent pathway has been reported in human umbilical vein epithelial cells (HUVECs), culminating in lysosome fusion.
claims.source: A similar noncanonical ATG dependent pathway has been reported in human umbilical vein epithelial cells (HUVECs), although it differs slightly in culminating in lysosome fusion (Clough et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Clough et al., 2016.

claims.claim: Indoleamine 2,3-dioxygenase (IDO1) restricts T. gondii growth by limiting L-tryptophan availability in human fibroblasts and monocyte-derived macrophages as well as in human-derived cell lines of myeloid, foreskin, liver, or cervix origin but not in cells lines originating from mesenchymal stem cells, the large intestine, or the umbilical endothelium.
claims.source: Finally, indoleamine 2,3-dioxygenase (IDO1) has been shown in vitro to restrict T. gondii growth by limiting L-tryptophan availability in human fibroblasts and monocyte-derived macrophages as well as in human-derived cell lines of myeloid, foreskin, liver, or cervix origin (e.g., HAP1s, HFFs, Huh7s, and HeLas) but not in cells lines originating from mesenchymal stem cells, the large intestine, or the umbilical endothelium (e.g., MSCs, CaCO2s, or HUVECs) (Qin et al., 2017; Bando et al., 2018; Pfefferkorn, 1984; Woodman et al., 1991; Dimier and Bout, 1997; Schmitz et al., 1989).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Qin et al., 2017; Bando et al., 2018; Pfefferkorn, 1984; Woodman et al., 1991; Dimier and Bout, 1997; Schmitz et al., 1989.

claims.claim: A549 cells were infected with CTG-GFP and the size of individual parasitophorous vacuoles (PVs), the number of vacuoles per field, and the percentage of vacuoles with a size consistent with containing ≥8 parasites were determined after 36 hr of culture.
claims.source: A549 lung epithelial cells were infected with CTG-GFP and the size of individual parasitophorous vacuoles (PVs), the number of vacuoles per field, and the percentage of vacuoles with a size consistent with containing ≥8 parasites were determined after 36 hr of culture (Figure 1A–C).
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental method and references Figure 1A-C showing the data.

claims.claim: CTG is a type III strain of T. gondii that is avirulent in mice and more susceptible to IFNγ-mediated restriction than other strains.
claims.source: CTG is a type III strain of T. gondii that is avirulent in mice and more susceptible to IFNγ-mediated restriction than other strains thus making it ideal for identifying individual ISGs which can restrict infection (Khaminets et al., 2010; Boothroyd and Grigg, 2002; Saeij et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Khaminets et al., 2010; Boothroyd and Grigg, 2002; Saeij et al., 2006.

claims.claim: A549 cells are highly permissive to transduction with VSV-G pseudotyped lentivirus and readily infected by T. gondii.
claims.source: A549 cells were used as they are highly permissive to transduction with our VSV-G pseudotyped lentivirus and readily infected by T. gondii.
claims.evidence: This is a justification for the choice of cell line based on experimental characteristics.

claims.claim: Transduction efficiency was high for most ISGs with 86% (357/414) of ISGs expressed in at least 50% of the cell population.
claims.source: Transduction efficiency was high for most ISGs with 86% (357/414) of ISGs expressed in at least 50% of the cell population and 50% of ISGs (205/414) expressed in 90% of the cell population (Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from the screen.

claims.claim: 50% of ISGs (205/414) were expressed in 90% of the cell population.
claims.source: Transduction efficiency was high for most ISGs with 86% (357/414) of ISGs expressed in at least 50% of the cell population and 50% of ISGs (205/414) expressed in 90% of the cell population (Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from the screen.

claims.claim: Three ISGs that restricted infection were found: IRF1, TRIM31, and RARRES3.
claims.source: Using this approach, we found three ISGs that restricted infection: IRF1, TRIM31, and RARRES3 (Figure 1E, Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from the screen shown in Figure 1E.

claims.claim: All hits were identified as significant by a two-way ANOVA (p<0.0001).
claims.source: All hits were identified as significant by a two-way ANOVA (p<0.0001).
claims.evidence: This describes the statistical analysis used to identify hits.

claims.claim: Six ISGs significantly promoted parasite growth, including IL7R, IFITM1, MX1, DHX58, RNF19B, and CNDP2.
claims.source: Interestingly, six ISGs significantly promoted parasite growth, including IL7R, IFITM1, MX1, DHX58, RNF19B, and CNDP2.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the screen.

claims.claim: IDO1 deficiency did not impair IFNγ-mediated restriction of CTG-GFP in A549 cells.
claims.source: Consistent with the results of our screen, IDO1 deficiency did not impair IFNγ-mediated restriction of CTG-GFP (Figure 1F).
claims.evidence: This is a result from experiments shown in Figure 1F.

claims.claim: The concentration of tryptophan used in the media for these experiments (16 µg/ml) was higher than what has been used previously to observe IDO1-mediated infection restriction.
claims.source: It is worth noting here that the concentration of tryptophan used in the media for these experiments (16 µg/ml) was higher than what has been used previously to observe IDO1-mediated infection restriction, which may prevent IDO1-mediated depletion of tryptophan (Pfefferkorn, 1984).
claims.evidence: This is a methodological note with citation to Pfefferkorn, 1984.

claims.claim: IDO1 does not play a major role in the restriction of T. gondii in A549 cells under the experimental conditions used in this study.
claims.source: Collectively, our results suggest that IDO1 does not play a major role in the restriction of T. gondii in A549 cells under the experimental conditions used in this study.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented.

claims.claim: Cells ectopically expressing IRF1, TRIM31, and RARRES3 expanded normally and showed similar viability compared to a luciferase control.
claims.source: Cells ectopically expressing IRF1, TRIM31, and RARRES3 expanded normally and showed similar viability compared to a luciferase control when stained with the live-dead stain SYTOX green, suggesting that the overexpression of these genes is not cytotoxic (Figure 2A–B).
claims.evidence: This is a result from experiments shown in Figure 2A-B.

claims.claim: Overexpression of IRF1, TRIM31, and RARRES3 is not cytotoxic.
claims.source: Cells ectopically expressing IRF1, TRIM31, and RARRES3 expanded normally and showed similar viability compared to a luciferase control when stained with the live-dead stain SYTOX green, suggesting that the overexpression of these genes is not cytotoxic (Figure 2A–B).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the viability data shown in Figure 2A-B.

claims.claim: RARRES3 and IRF1 ectopic expression resulted in a reduction in average vacuole size at 36 hr.
claims.source: RARRES3 and IRF1 ectopic expression resulted in a reduction in average vacuole size at 36 hr (Figure 2C–D).
claims.evidence: This is a result from experiments shown in Figure 2C-D.

claims.claim: At 96 hr, the total area infected per well was significantly lower for RARRES3 and IRF1 expressing cells compared to control.
claims.source: At 96 hr, the total area infected per well was significantly lower for RARRES3 and IRF1 expressing cells compared to control as was the average size of infection foci (Figure 2E–F).
claims.evidence: This is a result from experiments shown in Figure 2E-F.

claims.claim: The average size of infection foci at 96 hr was significantly lower for RARRES3 and IRF1 expressing cells compared to control.
claims.source: At 96 hr, the total area infected per well was significantly lower for RARRES3 and IRF1 expressing cells compared to control as was the average size of infection foci (Figure 2E–F).
claims.evidence: This is a result from experiments shown in Figure 2E-F.

claims.claim: TRIM31 had no significant effect on infection in validation experiments.
claims.source: TRIM31 had no significant effect on infection in validation experiments and it was not studied further.
claims.evidence: This is a result from validation experiments.

claims.claim: IRF1 has a known role in amplifying IFNγ-mediated transcription.
claims.source: IRF1 has a known role in amplifying IFNγ-mediated transcription, and its role relative to IFNγ is further explored below.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about IRF1 function.

claims.claim: RARRES3 is a small, 18.2 kDa single domain protein in the HRASLS subfamily.
claims.source: RARRES3 is a small, 18.2 kDa single domain protein in the HRASLS subfamily (Mardian et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Mardian et al., 2015.

claims.claim: RARRES3 has been shown to inhibit immunoproteasome expression in cancer cells.
claims.source: RARRES33 has been shown to inhibit immunoproteasome expression in cancer cells (Anderson et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Anderson et al., 2017.

claims.claim: RARRES3 displays phospholipase A1/2 activity in vitro.
claims.source: It displays phospholipase A1/2 activity in vitro and has been shown to suppress Ras signaling and promote apoptosis (Uyama et al., 2009; Tsai et al., 2007; Han et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Uyama et al., 2009; Tsai et al., 2007; Han et al., 2010.

claims.claim: RARRES3 has been shown to suppress Ras signaling and promote apoptosis.
claims.source: It displays phospholipase A1/2 activity in vitro and has been shown to suppress Ras signaling and promote apoptosis (Uyama et al., 2009; Tsai et al., 2007; Han et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Uyama et al., 2009; Tsai et al., 2007; Han et al., 2010.

claims.claim: RARRES3 was described by a previous screen to be antiviral.
claims.source: Although RARRES3 was described by a previous screen to be antiviral (Schoggins et al., 2014), it was not studied further and little is known about its involvement in immunity to other pathogens.
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Schoggins et al., 2014.

claims.claim: 160 genes were upregulated by IRF1 in A549 cells (FDR≤0.05, twofold).
claims.source: We identified 160 genes upregulated by IRF1 and 380 genes upregulated by IFNγ in A549 cells (FDR≤0.05, twofold) (Supplementary file 2).
claims.evidence: This is a result from RNA-seq analysis.

claims.claim: 380 genes were upregulated by IFNγ in A549 cells (FDR≤0.05, twofold).
claims.source: We identified 160 genes upregulated by IRF1 and 380 genes upregulated by IFNγ in A549 cells (FDR≤0.05, twofold) (Supplementary file 2).
claims.evidence: This is a result from RNA-seq analysis.

claims.claim: 41.1% (86/160) of IRF1 induced genes were represented by the ISG library.
claims.source: When we compared these gene lists with the ISG library with which we challenged T. gondii infection, we found that 41.1% (86/160) of IFNγ induced genes and 53.8% (156/380) of IRF1 induced genes were represented by the library (Supplementary file 3).
claims.evidence: This is a result from comparing RNA-seq data with the ISG library.

claims.claim: 53.8% (156/380) of IFNγ induced genes were represented by the ISG library.
claims.source: When we compared these gene lists with the ISG library with which we challenged T. gondii infection, we found that 41.1% (86/160) of IFNγ induced genes and 53.8% (156/380) of IRF1 induced genes were represented by the library (Supplementary file 3).
claims.evidence: This is a result from comparing RNA-seq data with the ISG library.

claims.claim: 69% of the top 100 strongest induced genes by IFNγ were represented in the ISG library.
claims.source: Notably, strongly induced ISGs were more commonly represented in the ISG library with 69% of the top 100 strongest induced genes by IFNγ and 67% of those induced by IRF1 being represented (Figure 3C, Supplementary file 3).
claims.evidence: This is a result from comparing RNA-seq data with the ISG library, shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: 67% of the top 100 strongest induced genes by IRF1 were represented in the ISG library.
claims.source: Notably, strongly induced ISGs were more commonly represented in the ISG library with 69% of the top 100 strongest induced genes by IFNγ and 67% of those induced by IRF1 being represented (Figure 3C, Supplementary file 3).
claims.evidence: This is a result from comparing RNA-seq data with the ISG library, shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: Gene ontology (GO) analysis for the lists of IRF1 and IFNγ induced genes revealed induction of very similar processes that were grouped into IFN signaling, immune response regulation, host defense, and antigen presentation.
claims.source: Gene ontology (GO) analysis for the lists of IRF1 and IFNγ induced genes revealed induction of very similar processes that were grouped into IFN signaling, immune response regulation, host defense, and antigen presentation (Figure 3D–E).
claims.evidence: This is a result from GO analysis shown in Figure 3D-E.

claims.claim: RARRES3 was strongly induced by both IRF1 and IFNγ treatment.
claims.source: Interestingly, RARRES3 was strongly induced by both IRF1 and IFNγ treatment.
claims.evidence: This is a result from RNA-seq analysis.

claims.claim: IRF1 expression strongly induces RARRES3 expression in human hepatoma and skin fibroblast derived cell lines.
claims.source: This is consistent with the previously reported finding that IRF1 expression strongly induces RARRES3 expression in human hepatoma and skin fibroblast derived cell lines (Schoggins et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Schoggins et al., 2011.

claims.claim: The same phenotypes were observed with RARRES3 ectopic expression irrespective of the presence of STAT1.
claims.source: The same phenotypes were observed with RARRES3 ectopic expression irrespective of the presence of STAT1, suggesting that decreased infection on overexpression of RARRES3 is not due to induction of IFNγ signaling (Figure 4C–F).
claims.evidence: This is a result from experiments in STAT1-/- cells shown in Figure 4C-F.

claims.claim: Decreased infection on overexpression of RARRES3 is not due to induction of IFNγ signaling.
claims.source: The same phenotypes were observed with RARRES3 ectopic expression irrespective of the presence of STAT1, suggesting that decreased infection on overexpression of RARRES3 is not due to induction of IFNγ signaling (Figure 4C–F).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the STAT1-/- experiments shown in Figure 4C-F.

claims.claim: RARRES3 ectopic expression resulted in a modest increase in the number of PVs observed at 36 hr in WT cells and was slightly more pronounced in STAT1−/− cells.
claims.source: Interestingly, we noticed that RARRES3 ectopic expression resulted in a modest increase in the number of PVs observed at 36 hr in WT cells and was slightly more pronounced in STAT1−/− cells (Figures 2C and 4C).
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the data shown in Figures 2C and 4C.

claims.claim: RARRES3 did not significantly impact luciferase expression for κB-, ISRE-, and GAS-luciferase reporters.
claims.source: RARRES3 did not significantly impact luciferase expression for any of the reporters tested (Figure 4G–J).
claims.evidence: This is a result from luciferase reporter assays shown in Figure 4G-J.

claims.claim: RARRES3 does not modulate immune signaling pathways.
claims.source: These findings suggest that RARRES3 does not modulate immune signaling pathways and instead plays a direct role in restricting infection.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the luciferase reporter and STAT1-/- experiments.

claims.claim: RARRES3 plays a direct role in restricting infection.
claims.source: These findings suggest that RARRES3 does not modulate immune signaling pathways and instead plays a direct role in restricting infection.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data.

claims.claim: The enzymatic activity of RARRES3 is necessary for restriction of infection.
claims.source: These data suggest that the enzymatic activity of RARRES3 is necessary for restriction of infection.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the catalytic mutant experiments shown in Figure 5A-B.

claims.claim: RARRES3 deficiency partially alleviated IFNγ-mediated restriction of CTG-GFP infection.
claims.source: However, RARRES3 deficiency partially alleviated IFNγ-mediated restriction of CTG-GFP infection and this deficiency was complemented with RARRES3 ectopic expression (Figure 5C–D).
claims.evidence: This is a result from experiments in RARRES3-/- cells shown in Figure 5C-D.

claims.claim: RARRES3 deficiency was complemented with RARRES3 ectopic expression.
claims.source: However, RARRES3 deficiency partially alleviated IFNγ-mediated restriction of CTG-GFP infection and this deficiency was complemented with RARRES3 ectopic expression (Figure 5C–D).
claims.evidence: This is a result from complementation experiments shown in Figure 5C-D.

claims.claim: Loss of RARRES3 did not impact IRF1-mediated restriction of infection.
claims.source: However, loss of RARRES3 did not impact IRF1-mediated restriction of infection (Figure 5E).
claims.evidence: This is a result from experiments shown in Figure 5E.

claims.claim: IRF1-mediated infection restriction is RARRES3 independent or involves multiple factors with RARRES3 playing a redundant role.
claims.source: This suggests that either IRF1-mediated infection restriction is RARRES3 independent or involves multiple factors with RARRES3 playing a redundant role in the process of restricting growth.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the IRF1 experiments in RARRES3-/- cells.

claims.claim: RARRES3 had no impact on the infection of type I (RH88) or type II (Me49) strains of T. gondii.
claims.source: However, RARRES3 had no impact on the infection of either of these two strains (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is a result from experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

results.result: A high-throughput screen of 414 IFNγ-induced ISGs identified three genes (IRF1, TRIM31, and RARRES3) that restrict T. gondii CTG strain infection in A549 cells. The screen achieved high transduction efficiency (86% of ISGs expressed in ≥50% of cells) and used automated microscopy to quantify infection parameters at 36 hours post-infection.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C44-C50 describe the screening methodology and primary hits. The experimental design is clearly described with appropriate controls, statistical analysis (two-way ANOVA, p<0.0001), and high transduction efficiency documented. The identification of three restrictive ISGs is supported by quantitative imaging data shown in Figure 1E.

results.result: Six ISGs (IL7R, IFITM1, MX1, DHX58, RNF19B, and CNDP2) significantly promoted parasite growth in the screen.
results.evaluation: Claim C51 reports ISGs that enhanced infection, identified with the same statistical rigor as restrictive ISGs. While not the focus of follow-up studies, this finding is supported by the screening data and represents a valid observation from the experimental approach.

results.result: IDO1 does not play a major role in restricting T. gondii in A549 cells under the experimental conditions used (16 µg/ml tryptophan, high IFNγ doses).
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C54 address why IDO1 was not identified in the screen. IDO1-/- cells showed no impairment in IFNγ-mediated restriction (Figure 1F with western blot confirmation). The authors appropriately note that high tryptophan concentration may prevent IDO1-mediated depletion, providing context for the negative result.

results.result: Validation experiments confirmed that RARRES3 and IRF1 ectopic expression restrict T. gondii infection without cytotoxicity, while TRIM31 showed no significant effect. RARRES3 and IRF1 reduced vacuole size at 36 hr and total infected area at 96 hr.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C60 describe validation of screen hits. Cell viability data (Figure 2A-B) demonstrates lack of cytotoxicity. Quantitative infection data at 36 hr and 96 hr (Figure 2C-F) with appropriate statistical analysis confirms restriction by RARRES3 and IRF1. The negative result for TRIM31 is appropriately reported.

results.result: RNA-seq analysis revealed that IRF1 induces 160 genes while IFNγ induces 380 genes in A549 cells (FDR≤0.05, ≥2-fold). The ISG library represented 41.1% of IRF1-induced and 53.8% of IFNγ-induced genes, with better coverage of strongly induced genes (67-69% of top 100). Both treatments induced similar biological processes including IFN signaling and immune response. RARRES3 was strongly induced by both IRF1 and IFNγ.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C74 present RNA-seq results with appropriate statistical thresholds (FDR≤0.05, 2-fold change). The comparison with the ISG library is quantitative and shows reasonable coverage, particularly for highly induced genes. GO analysis (Figure 3D-E) supports functional similarity. The finding that RARRES3 is induced by both treatments connects to the screening results.

results.result: RARRES3 restricts infection independently of STAT1-mediated IFNγ signaling and does not modulate immune signaling pathways (NF-κB, ISRE, GAS). The same restriction phenotypes were observed in STAT1-/- cells, and RARRES3 did not affect luciferase reporters for immune signaling.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C81 demonstrate RARRES3 acts independently of canonical IFN signaling. Experiments in STAT1-/- cells (Figure 4C-F) with confirmed knockout (Figure 4A-B) show identical phenotypes. Luciferase reporter assays (Figure 4G-J) provide additional evidence that RARRES3 does not modulate immune signaling. The inference that RARRES3 plays a direct role is well-supported.

results.result: The enzymatic (phospholipase) activity of RARRES3 is necessary for restriction of infection, as catalytic mutants (C113A, C113S) failed to restrict infection despite strong expression.
results.evaluation: Claim C82 is supported by experiments with catalytic mutants (Figure 5A-B). Both C113A and C113S mutants lost restrictive activity despite being expressed at higher levels than wild-type (western blot confirmation). This structure-function analysis provides mechanistic insight into RARRES3 function.

results.result: Endogenous RARRES3 contributes to IFNγ-mediated restriction of CTG infection. RARRES3-/- cells showed partial alleviation of IFNγ-mediated restriction that was complemented by RARRES3 expression. However, RARRES3 loss did not affect IRF1-mediated restriction, suggesting IRF1 acts through multiple factors or RARRES3 plays a redundant role.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C86 demonstrate physiological relevance using RARRES3-/- cells. The partial rescue phenotype (Figure 5C-D) with complementation validates the knockout. The lack of effect on IRF1-mediated restriction (Figure 5E) is appropriately interpreted as evidence for redundancy or multiple pathways, consistent with the RNA-seq data showing IRF1 induces many genes.

results.result: RARRES3 had no impact on infection by type I (RH88) or type II (Me49) T. gondii strains, suggesting strain-specific susceptibility possibly due to differential virulence factor expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C87-C88 report negative results for other strains (Figure 5—supplement 1). The data clearly show no effect on RH88 or Me49. The speculation about virulence factors (C88) is appropriately presented as a hypothesis with supporting citations, not as a demonstrated mechanism.

results.result: RARRES3 induces premature parasite egress. RARRES3 expression increased LDH release during infection, which was blocked by Compound 1 (PKG inhibitor), indicating egress-dependent cell lysis. Live imaging confirmed parasites egressed significantly earlier in RARRES3-expressing cells (p<0.0001).
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C93 establish the premature egress mechanism. LDH assays (Figure 6A-B) show increased release blocked by Compound 1, and propidium iodide staining (Figure 6—supplement 1A) confirms cells remain intact with PKG inhibition. Live imaging (Figure 6C, Videos 1-2) provides direct temporal evidence with appropriate statistics (two-way ANOVA). The inference that LDH release is due to egress is well-supported.

results.result: RARRES3-induced premature egress occurs independently of host cell death pathways. Compound 1 prevented cell loss during infection, and a panel of cell death inhibitors (targeting apoptosis, necroptosis, pyroptosis) failed to block LDH release, except GSK'872 which likely induced apoptosis. These findings indicate RARRES3 triggers egress through a mechanism distinct from cell death induction.
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C100 systematically rule out cell death as the trigger for egress. Extended time course with Compound 1 (Figure 6E, Figure 6—supplement 1B-C) shows no cell death even at 72 hr when egress is blocked. Comprehensive testing of cell death inhibitors (Figure 6F) with appropriate controls strengthens the conclusion. The interpretation that GSK'872 effects are due to RIP3 inhibition-induced apoptosis is reasonable.

results.result: RARRES3 restricts CTG infection in HFF cells and contributes to IFNγ-dependent premature egress in this cell type. RARRES3-/- HFFs showed partial reduction in IFNγ-dependent cell death and infection restriction. Compound 1 completely blocked cell death, confirming PKG-dependent egress causes cell lysis in HFFs.
results.evaluation: Claims C101-C106 extend findings to a second cell line. Ectopic expression (Figure 7A-B) and knockout experiments (Figure 7C-D) show consistent restriction phenotypes. The partial phenotype in RARRES3-/- HFFs indicates RARRES3 is one of multiple factors in this cell type. Compound 1 experiments (Figure 7E, Figure 6—supplement 1D-F) confirm the egress mechanism operates in HFFs.

results.result: RARRES3 overexpression promotes premature parasite egress independently of host cell death pathways in multiple cell lines, which presumably stunts parasite growth leading to reduced infection overall.
results.evaluation: Claims C107-C108 synthesize findings from A549 and HFF experiments. The conclusion that egress is cell death-independent is well-supported by data from both cell types. The inference that premature egress stunts growth (C108) is reasonable given the observed reduction in vacuole size and infection spread, though direct measurement of parasite numbers per vacuole would strengthen this claim.

results.result: IRF1 restricts T. gondii infection likely through collective action of multiple downstream ISGs. IRF1-induced genes were largely a subset of IFNγ-induced genes including RARRES3, but IRF1-mediated restriction was RARRES3-independent.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C7, C61, C113-C114 characterize IRF1's mechanism. The screen identified IRF1 as restrictive (Figure 1E), RNA-seq showed it induces a subset of IFNγ genes (Figure 3), and genetic experiments showed RARRES3-independence (Figure 5E). The inference that IRF1 works through multiple ISGs is well-supported by the RNA-seq data showing 160 induced genes and the lack of dependence on the single identified ISG (RARRES3).

results.result: The limited number of ISGs capable of restricting T. gondii infection when individually expressed (only 2-3 out of 414) suggests that IFNγ-mediated immunity to T. gondii is a complex, multifactorial process requiring cooperation of multiple ISGs or cellular proteins.
results.evaluation: Claims C9, C115, C134 interpret the overall screening results. The observation that only 2-3 ISGs out of 414 restrict infection when individually expressed is clearly documented. The inference that this indicates complexity and requirement for multiple factors is reasonable and consistent with the IRF1 results. This interpretation is strengthened by comparison to viral/bacterial screens that typically identify more hits.

results.result: Screens of ISGs against viruses and bacteria typically identify 2-3 times more restrictive factors than found in this T. gondii screen. This difference may reflect T. gondii's separation from host cytoplasm via the PVM, its relative autonomy from host machinery, or the complexity of controlling eukaryotic pathogens compared to viruses.
results.evaluation: Claims C129-C133, C116 contextualize results through comparison with other pathogen screens. The comparison is supported by multiple citations to prior screens. The proposed explanations (PVM barrier, parasite autonomy, pathogen complexity) are presented as speculation with appropriate caveats. These are reasonable hypotheses that warrant future investigation.

results.result: The mechanism by which RARRES3 induces premature egress is unclear, though its phospholipase A1/A2 activity may alter cellular lipid pools. Increases in phosphatidic acid and lecithin:cholesterol acyltransferase activity have been shown to trigger T. gondii egress.
results.evaluation: Claims C117-C120 acknowledge knowledge gaps and propose mechanisms. C117 correctly states the mechanism is unclear. C118 is speculation about lipid pool alterations, supported by the requirement for catalytic activity but lacking direct evidence. C119-C120 cite prior work on lipid-triggered egress, providing context but not demonstrating RARRES3 acts through these pathways. Further experiments are needed to test these hypotheses.
